title.en: Look up, a kite is flying

text.en: Think of a windy afternoon when the sky fills with kites of every colour. Have you ever flown one, or just stood watching one climb higher and higher? This short poem by Daphne Lister is about a child who watches kites and dreams of riding one up into the sky.

The chapter opens with questions about your own kite memories: where and when you saw a kite, what colours, shape and tail it had, and what you felt on seeing it in the sky. You are asked to watch videos of kite festivals with your teacher, say what the people were doing, and decide what kind of kite you would like to fly. A picture task asks you to complete sentences using words such as windy, kite, flying, birds, sky, looking and has ribbons. The weather in the picture is windy, the kite is flying high, and the child is looking up from below.
The poem is a child's daydream. The kites flying in the wind-whipped sky look like coloured birds. The child wishes to be small and as light as air, so that a kite could carry the child up into the sky. The child imagines drifting on the paper wings of the kite and hearing the songs that the wild wind sings. From up there the child could look down at the park and the rooftops of the town, and the people below would stand and stare and wish they were in the child's place, high in the air.
The child is looking at the kites, so that statement is true, and the kites look like birds of different colours, which is also true. It was not a rainy day. The sky is windy, so a statement that says it was raining is false. The child wishes to climb on a kite and ride it, and knows it would be fun, so these are true. The kite has paper wings, so a statement that says it is made of cloth and plastic is false. The child wants to look down at the park and rooftops from the kite, not from a rooftop, and the people below stare, so the rooftop statement is false.
A simile compares two things using the words like or as. The poet compares kites to coloured birds with like, and the child wishes to be as light as air with as. These pictures help us imagine the scene. Alliteration is the repeating of the same beginning consonant sound in nearby words. In the first stanza wind and whipped begin with the w sound, and in the third stanza wild and wind do the same. Big bright blue bag and funny fan are other examples. The poet repeats the word high in the last stanza to tell us that the kite is flying very high. Rhyming words come at the ends of lines. In this poem fly rhymes with sky, air with there, wings with sings, down with town, and stare with air.
The parts of a kite named in the book are the nose, spine, cover, kite line, tail and reel. The tip of a kite is called the nose. In the little conversation, Bina likes the long tail of her kite, Saroj's kite has a bright cover and a black spine, and the kite line is wound on the reel. The poet uses fly and drift for the kite. Drift means to move slowly and gently, like floating. Glide is a smooth, easy movement, dive is a quick drop downward, soar is a high upward flight, swoop is a sudden sweep down, and circle is a movement round and round. Expressions in the poem are up in the air, look right down, stay up there and stand and stare. Try making your own sentences with them.
A cinquain is a five-line poem about a person, a place or a thing. Line one is one noun, line two has two describing words, line three has three action words, line four has two words that tell how the action happens, and line five is one word that means the same as the subject. The book shows an example: kite, then pretty and colourful, then flying, floating and soaring, then quickly and happily, and last paper-bird. Now write a cinquain of your own about anything you like, following the same five-line pattern.
In the listening passage the Kite Festival takes place during Makar Sankranti in January and is called Uttarayan in Western India. Gujarat is the main centre, but it is also celebrated in Rajasthan and Telangana. In Karnataka the Tourism Department organises it once a year, and Punjab flies kites at Baisakhi and Basant Panchami. In the exercise, the wrong statements are June instead of January, Eastern India instead of Western, Maharashtra instead of Rajasthan, and Earth Day instead of the other festivals. Listen again to correct them. For speaking, share a kite-flying experience with where, when, why and how. For writing, imagine you are a kite and write about 100 words titled I am a Kite, covering your shape, colours, friends and a message for humans. Kites are mentioned in ancient Indian texts. The thirteenth-century Marathi saint and poet Namadeva called a kite a gudi, made from kaagad, which means paper. Kite types you can explore are parafoil, delta, diamond-shaped, rokkaku and box kites.

problem.en: Match each simile word with what it compares: like coloured birds; as light as air.

text.en: Find the comparing word in each phrase.

why.en: Like in the first phrase and as in the second show that these are similes.

text.en: Say what is compared.

why.en: Kites are compared to coloured birds, and the child to something very light, air.

problem.en: Fill in the cinquain pattern for the word cat.

text.en: Line one: the noun.
Add two describing words, three action words, two how-words and a synonym.

why.en: For example furry, soft; running, jumping, purring; quickly, quietly; kitten.

prompt.en: Explain the poem The Kites in your own words and name one device the poet uses.

requiredIdeas.en: A child watches kites in a windy sky.
The child wishes to ride a kite and see the town from above.
The people below stare and wish to be there.
Devices include simile, alliteration, repetition and rhyme.

commonMisconceptions.en: The child is flying a kite from a rooftop.
The poem is about a rainy day.

points.en: The poem is a child's daydream about riding a kite high above the town.
A simile compares using like or as, and alliteration repeats a starting sound.
The nose, spine, cover, kite line, tail and reel are parts of a kite.
Drift, glide, soar, dive, swoop and circle tell how kites move.
A cinquain is a five-line poem with a fixed pattern.
